_doc: The replication ledger's findings. Each finding is one claim, its original study and every replication attempt filed so far. No standing is typed here: standing.js computes it from the attempts. Citations carry a DOI wherever one exists, checked against Crossref by `node worker/cli.mjs verify`; new attempts are appended with `node worker/cli.mjs add`, never by hand-editing a standing. Summaries are plain words with no numbers: a number enters only from the source itself.

findings.name: Ego depletion
findings.claim: Exerting self-control on one task drains a limited resource, so self-control on a following task is weaker.

original.authors: Baumeister RF, Bratslavsky E, Muraven M, Tice DM
original.title: Ego depletion: is the active self a limited resource?
original.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

cite.authors: Hagger MS, Chatzisarantis NLD, Alberts H, et al.
cite.title: A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect

replications.summary: Across many laboratories following one preregistered protocol, the depletion effect was close to zero.

cite.authors: Vohs KD, Schmeichel BJ, Lohmann S, et al.
cite.title: A multisite preregistered paradigmatic test of the ego-depletion effect

replications.summary: A second multisite test, designed with proponents of the effect, again found an effect near zero.

findings.name: Facial feedback (pen in the mouth)
findings.claim: Holding a pen in the teeth, which forces a smile, makes cartoons seem funnier than holding it in the lips.

original.authors: Strack F, Martin LL, Stepper S
original.title: Inhibiting and facilitating conditions of the human smile: a nonobtrusive test of the facial feedback hypothesis
original.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

cite.authors: Wagenmakers EJ, Beek T, Dijkhoff L, et al.
cite.title: Registered Replication Report: Strack, Martin, & Stepper (1988)

replications.summary: Seventeen laboratories ran the original pen procedure and together found no reliable difference in rated funniness.

cite.authors: Coles NA, March DS, Marmolejo-Ramos F, et al.
cite.title: A multi-lab test of the facial feedback hypothesis by the Many Smiles Collaboration

replications.summary: Posed smiling raised reported happiness in some tasks but not all, so whether facial feedback shows up depends on how the expression is produced.

findings.name: Power posing
findings.claim: Holding an expansive 'power pose' for a couple of minutes raises testosterone, lowers cortisol and increases risk taking.

original.authors: Carney DR, Cuddy AJC, Yap AJ
original.title: Power posing: brief nonverbal displays affect neuroendocrine levels and risk tolerance

cite.authors: Ranehill E, Dreber A, Johannesson M, Leiberg S, Sul S, Weber RA
cite.title: Assessing the robustness of power posing: no effect on hormones and risk tolerance in a large sample of men and women

replications.summary: In a much larger sample, power poses changed neither hormone levels nor risk taking, though people reported feeling more powerful.

findings.name: Elderly priming (slow walking)
findings.claim: Unscrambling sentences with words about old age makes people walk more slowly down a corridor afterwards.

original.authors: Bargh JA, Chen M, Burrows L
original.title: Automaticity of social behavior: direct effects of trait construct and stereotype activation on action
original.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

cite.authors: Doyen S, Klein O, Pichon CL, Cleeremans A
cite.title: Behavioral priming: it's all in the mind, but whose mind?

replications.summary: Timed by infrared sensors, primed participants did not walk more slowly; slowing appeared only when the experimenters expected it.

findings.name: Anchoring
findings.claim: An arbitrary number shown before an estimate pulls the estimate toward it.

original.authors: Tversky A, Kahneman D
original.title: Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases

cite.authors: Klein RA, Ratliff KA, Vianello M, et al.
cite.title: Investigating variation in replicability: a "many labs" replication project

replications.summary: Anchoring replicated strongly in nearly every one of the many participating samples.

findings.name: Gain and loss framing
findings.claim: People choose the sure option when outcomes are framed as lives saved and the gamble when the same outcomes are framed as lives lost.

original.authors: Tversky A, Kahneman D
original.title: The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice

cite.authors: Klein RA, Ratliff KA, Vianello M, et al.
cite.title: Investigating variation in replicability: a "many labs" replication project

replications.summary: The framing effect replicated across the participating samples.

findings.name: The testing effect
findings.claim: Practising retrieval by testing yourself leads to better long-term retention than spending the same time restudying.

original.authors: Roediger HL, Karpicke JD
original.title: Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention

cite.authors: Rowland CA
cite.title: The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: a meta-analytic review of the testing effect

replications.summary: Across many experiments, testing beat restudying for later retention, with the size of the benefit depending on conditions such as feedback.

findings.name: The marshmallow test predicts later success
findings.claim: How long a preschooler waits for a second treat predicts their later academic competence.

original.authors: Shoda Y, Mischel W, Peake PK
original.title: Predicting adolescent cognitive and self-regulatory competencies from preschool delay of gratification: identifying diagnostic conditions

findings.query: delay of gratification marshmallow later outcomes replication

cite.authors: Watts TW, Duncan GJ, Quan H
cite.title: Revisiting the marshmallow test: a conceptual replication investigating links between early delay of gratification and later outcomes

replications.summary: In a larger and more diverse sample, the link with later achievement was much smaller and shrank further once family background and early ability were accounted for.

findings.name: Obedience to authority (Milgram)
findings.claim: Most ordinary people will follow an experimenter's instructions to give what they believe are painful electric shocks to another person.

original.authors: Milgram S
original.title: Behavioral study of obedience
original.venue: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology

cite.authors: Burger JM
cite.title: Replicating Milgram: would people still obey today?

replications.summary: A partial replication that stopped at an earlier point for ethical reasons found obedience rates only slightly below Milgram's.

cite.authors: Doliński D, Grzyb T, Folwarczny M, et al.
cite.title: Would you deliver an electric shock in 2015? Obedience in the experimental paradigm developed by Stanley Milgram in the 50 years following the original studies

replications.summary: A Polish replication of the shortened procedure again found that most participants obeyed.

findings.name: Stanford prison experiment
findings.claim: Ordinary people assigned the role of guard will spontaneously become abusive toward people assigned the role of prisoner.

original.authors: Haney C, Banks C, Zimbardo P
original.title: Interpersonal dynamics in a simulated prison
original.venue: International Journal of Criminology and Penology
original.note: no DOI registered for this journal

cite.authors: Reicher S, Haslam SA
cite.title: Rethinking the psychology of tyranny: the BBC prison study

replications.summary: In a televised prison study without instructions to be tough, guards did not slide into tyranny on their own; group identification shaped what happened.

findings.name: Hormone therapy protects the heart
findings.claim: Postmenopausal hormone therapy lowers the risk of coronary heart disease.

original.authors: Stampfer MJ, Colditz GA, Willett WC, et al.
original.title: Postmenopausal estrogen therapy and cardiovascular disease: ten-year follow-up from the Nurses' Health Study

findings.query: hormone replacement therapy coronary heart disease randomized trial

cite.authors: Hulley S, Grady D, Bush T, et al.
cite.title: Randomized trial of estrogen plus progestin for secondary prevention of coronary heart disease in postmenopausal women

replications.summary: In women with existing heart disease, hormone therapy did not reduce coronary events.

cite.authors: Writing Group for the Women's Health Initiative Investigators
cite.title: Risks and benefits of estrogen plus progestin in healthy postmenopausal women: principal results from the Women's Health Initiative randomized controlled trial

replications.summary: The large randomized trial was stopped early: coronary heart disease was more common, not less, among women given hormones.

findings.name: Beta-carotene prevents lung cancer
findings.claim: Eating more beta-carotene, or taking it as a supplement, lowers the risk of cancer, especially lung cancer.

original.authors: Peto R, Doll R, Buckley JD, Sporn MB
original.title: Can dietary beta-carotene materially reduce human cancer rates?

findings.query: beta-carotene supplementation lung cancer randomized trial

cite.authors: Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta Carotene Cancer Prevention Study Group
cite.title: The effect of vitamin E and beta carotene on the incidence of lung cancer and other cancers in male smokers

replications.summary: Among male smokers, beta-carotene supplements were followed by more lung cancer, not less.

cite.authors: Omenn GS, Goodman GE, Thornquist MD, et al.
cite.title: Effects of a combination of beta carotene and vitamin A on lung cancer and cardiovascular disease

replications.summary: The CARET trial was stopped early because the supplement group had more lung cancer and more deaths.

findings.name: Vitamin E protects the heart
findings.claim: Taking vitamin E supplements lowers the risk of coronary heart disease.

original.authors: Stampfer MJ, Hennekens CH, Manson JE, Colditz GA, Rosner B, Willett WC
original.title: Vitamin E consumption and the risk of coronary disease in women

findings.query: vitamin E supplementation cardiovascular randomized trial

cite.authors: Heart Outcomes Prevention Evaluation Study Investigators; Yusuf S, Dagenais G, Pogue J, Bosch J, Sleight P
cite.title: Vitamin E supplementation and cardiovascular events in high-risk patients

replications.summary: In people at high cardiovascular risk, vitamin E had no apparent effect on heart attacks, strokes or cardiovascular death.

findings.name: Statins reduce deaths in people with heart disease
findings.claim: Lowering cholesterol with a statin reduces deaths and major coronary events in people with coronary heart disease.

original.authors: Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study Group
original.title: Randomised trial of cholesterol lowering in 4444 patients with coronary heart disease: the Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study (4S)

cite.authors: Heart Protection Study Collaborative Group
cite.title: MRC/BHF Heart Protection Study of cholesterol lowering with simvastatin in 20,536 high-risk individuals: a randomised placebo-controlled trial

replications.summary: A much larger trial in high-risk people found fewer deaths and fewer major vascular events with simvastatin.

cite.authors: Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' (CTT) Collaboration
cite.title: Efficacy and safety of more intensive lowering of LDL cholesterol: a meta-analysis of data from 170,000 participants in 26 randomised trials

replications.summary: Pooling the randomised trials, lowering LDL cholesterol with statins reduced major vascular events.

findings.name: Hydroxychloroquine treats COVID-19
findings.claim: Hydroxychloroquine helps patients with COVID-19 clear the virus and recover.

original.authors: Gautret P, Lagier JC, Parola P, et al.
original.title: Hydroxychloroquine and azithromycin as a treatment of COVID-19: results of an open-label non-randomized clinical trial

cite.authors: RECOVERY Collaborative Group
cite.title: Effect of hydroxychloroquine in hospitalized patients with Covid-19

replications.summary: In a large randomized trial of hospitalized patients, hydroxychloroquine did not lower deaths.

findings.name: Dexamethasone saves lives in severe COVID-19
findings.claim: Dexamethasone lowers deaths among hospitalized COVID-19 patients who need oxygen or ventilation.

original.authors: RECOVERY Collaborative Group
original.title: Dexamethasone in hospitalized patients with Covid-19

cite.authors: WHO Rapid Evidence Appraisal for COVID-19 Therapies (REACT) Working Group
cite.title: Association between administration of systemic corticosteroids and mortality among critically ill patients with COVID-19: a meta-analysis

replications.summary: A prospective meta-analysis of randomized trials found lower mortality with corticosteroids in critically ill patients.

findings.name: Growth falls sharply above 90% public debt
findings.claim: Countries whose public debt exceeds about 90 percent of GDP see much slower economic growth.

original.authors: Reinhart CM, Rogoff KS
original.title: Growth in a time of debt

findings.query: public debt growth threshold Reinhart Rogoff reanalysis

cite.authors: Herndon T, Ash M, Pollin R
cite.title: Does high public debt consistently stifle economic growth? A critique of Reinhart and Rogoff

replications.summary: Reanalysing the same data, with a spreadsheet error, selective exclusions and the weighting corrected, found no sharp drop in growth above the threshold.

findings.name: Microcredit lifts household consumption
findings.claim: Small loans to poor households, especially to women, raise household consumption.

original.authors: Pitt MM, Khandker SR
original.title: The impact of group-based credit programs on poor households in Bangladesh: does the gender of participants matter?

cite.authors: Roodman D, Morduch J
cite.title: The impact of microcredit on the poor in Bangladesh: revisiting the evidence

replications.summary: Replicating the analysis on the original data, the authors could not support the conclusion that the loans raised consumption.

cite.authors: Banerjee A, Karlan D, Zinman J
cite.title: Six randomized evaluations of microcredit: introduction and further steps

replications.summary: Six randomized evaluations on several continents found modestly positive but not transformative effects, with no clear rise in average consumption.

findings.name: A minimum wage rise did not cut fast-food jobs
findings.claim: New Jersey's 1992 minimum wage increase did not reduce employment in fast-food restaurants compared with neighbouring Pennsylvania.

original.authors: Card D, Krueger AB
original.title: Minimum wages and employment: a case study of the fast-food industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania
original.note: AER issues of 1994 carry no DOI

findings.query: New Jersey minimum wage fast food employment Card Krueger

cite.authors: Neumark D, Wascher W
cite.title: Minimum wages and employment: a case study of the fast-food industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania: comment

replications.summary: Using restaurants' own payroll records instead of a phone survey, the comment found employment fell in New Jersey relative to Pennsylvania.

cite.authors: Card D, Krueger AB
cite.title: Minimum wages and employment: a case study of the fast-food industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania: reply

replications.summary: Using official employment records for the same period, the reply again found no fall in New Jersey employment relative to Pennsylvania.

findings.name: School deworming raises attendance
findings.claim: Treating schoolchildren for intestinal worms raises school attendance, including among untreated children nearby.

original.authors: Miguel E, Kremer M
original.title: Worms: identifying impacts on education and health in the presence of treatment externalities

cite.authors: Aiken AM, Davey C, Hargreaves JR, Hayes RJ
cite.title: Re-analysis of health and educational impacts of a school-based deworming programme in western Kenya: a pure replication

replications.summary: Rerunning the original analysis found coding errors; with them corrected, some effects held while the spillover effect on nearby schools largely did not.

cite.authors: Davey C, Aiken AM, Hayes RJ, Hargreaves JR
cite.title: Re-analysis of health and educational impacts of a school-based deworming programme in western Kenya: a statistical replication of a cluster quasi-randomized stepped-wedge trial

replications.summary: Analysing the data with epidemiological methods set out in advance, the attendance effect depended on analytic choices and was weaker under some of them.

findings.name: Cold fusion
findings.claim: Electrolysis of heavy water with a palladium electrode at room temperature produces nuclear fusion and excess heat.

original.authors: Fleischmann M, Pons S
original.title: Electrochemically induced nuclear fusion of deuterium
original.venue: Journal of Electroanalytical Chemistry and Interfacial Electrochemistry

cite.authors: Lewis NS, Barnes CA, Heben MJ, et al.
cite.title: Searches for low-temperature nuclear fusion of deuterium in palladium

replications.summary: Careful calorimetry and searches for neutrons, gamma rays and tritium found no evidence of fusion or excess heat.

findings.name: Faster-than-light neutrinos
findings.claim: Neutrinos sent from CERN to Gran Sasso arrived slightly faster than light would.

original.authors: OPERA Collaboration; Adam T, et al.
original.title: Measurement of the neutrino velocity with the OPERA detector in the CNGS beam
original.note: first version of the preprint, as announced; later versions corrected the result

cite.authors: ICARUS Collaboration; Antonello M, et al.
cite.title: Measurement of the neutrino velocity with the ICARUS detector at the CNGS beam

replications.summary: An independent detector on the same beam found neutrino arrival times consistent with the speed of light; the original anomaly was traced to equipment faults.

findings.name: Discovery of a Higgs-like boson
findings.claim: A new boson with a mass near 125 GeV, consistent with the Standard Model Higgs boson, is produced at the Large Hadron Collider.

original.authors: ATLAS Collaboration
original.title: Observation of a new particle in the search for the Standard Model Higgs boson with the ATLAS detector at the LHC

cite.authors: CMS Collaboration
cite.title: Observation of a new boson at a mass of 125 GeV with the CMS experiment at the LHC

replications.summary: An independent detector and team observed the same new particle at the same mass.

findings.name: STAP cells
findings.claim: Exposing ordinary body cells to a mild stress such as acid turns them into pluripotent stem cells.

original.authors: Obokata H, Wakayama T, Sasai Y, et al.
original.title: Stimulus-triggered fate conversion of somatic cells into pluripotency

cite.authors: De Los Angeles A, Ferrari F, Fujiwara Y, et al.
cite.title: Failure to replicate the STAP cell phenomenon

replications.summary: Many attempts across several laboratories produced no pluripotent cells by the published method.

findings.name: Arsenic life
findings.claim: The bacterium GFAJ-1 can substitute arsenic for phosphorus and build it into its DNA.

original.authors: Wolfe-Simon F, Blum JS, Kulp TR, et al.
original.title: A bacterium that can grow by using arsenic instead of phosphorus

cite.authors: Reaves ML, Sinha S, Rabinowitz JD, Kruglyak L, Redfield RJ
cite.title: Absence of detectable arsenate in DNA from arsenate-grown GFAJ-1 cells

replications.summary: Purified DNA from cells grown with arsenate contained no detectable arsenate.

cite.authors: Erb TJ, Kiefer P, Hattendorf B, Günther D, Vorholt JA
cite.title: GFAJ-1 is an arsenate-resistant, phosphate-dependent organism

replications.summary: The bacterium still needed phosphate to grow; it tolerated arsenate rather than using it in place of phosphorus.

projects.what: Replicated 100 studies from three psychology journals

cite.authors: Open Science Collaboration
cite.title: Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science

projects.what: Replicated 28 classic and contemporary findings across many samples and settings

cite.authors: Klein RA, Vianello M, Hasselman F, et al.
cite.title: Many Labs 2: investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings
cite.venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science

cite.authors: Camerer CF, Dreber A, Forsell E, et al.
cite.title: Evaluating replicability of laboratory experiments in economics

projects.what: Replicated 21 social science experiments published in Nature and Science

cite.authors: Camerer CF, Dreber A, Holzmeister F, et al.
cite.title: Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science between 2010 and 2015

projects.what: Attempted to replicate experiments from high-impact preclinical cancer biology papers

cite.authors: Errington TM, Mathur M, Soderberg CK, et al.
cite.title: Investigating the replicability of preclinical cancer biology

projects.what: Followed up highly cited clinical studies to see how often later research contradicted or weakened them

cite.authors: Ioannidis JPA
cite.title: Contradicted and initially stronger effects in highly cited clinical research
